hazards.air-hose-chips: You blew the chips off with the air hose. Compressed air drives a chip through skin and into an eye, throws coolant mist into the air you are breathing, and packs swarf into the ways where it scores them.
hazards.bare-hand-chips: You pulled the chip nest off with a bare hand. Machining chips are a continuous razor at the temperature they came off the cut, and a stringer wrapped on a finger takes the finger with it if the spindle moves.
hazards.cycle-door-open: You pressed cycle start with the door open. The interlock is the only thing between the operator and a part that comes out of the vise at cutting speed; defeating it is the classic machine-shop fatality.
hazards.hand-in-envelope: You reached into the work envelope with the spindle live. A machining centre restarts on a queued command and a tool at four thousand revolutions does not care what is in the way; the door interlock exists because hands are faster than judgement and slower than a spindle.

interrupts.alert: A coworker leans in through the open door to point at something on the print, well inside the tool's swept path while the dry run is still moving.
interrupts.cue: Somebody's leaning into the envelope while the tool is still sweeping.
interrupts.missNote: Nobody froze it. The head kept travelling its programmed path a foot from a coworker leaning into the envelope to talk — a dry run only proves the program, it does not guarantee the tool stays clear of a person standing where it happens to swing.
interrupts.why: The dry run moves the real toolpath, just without the feed engaged into stock — the spindle is live and the head is travelling exactly where it will travel under program. A body inside that swept path while nobody has stopped the motion is one function key away from being where the tool goes next.
interrupts.wrongNote: That doesn't stop the head from moving — hit the spindle stop before anyone reaches in any further.

interrupts.alert: The enclosure's air curtain catches the setup sheet and slides it off the bench toward the chip pan, right as you're watching the dry run instead of the bench.
interrupts.cue: The setup sheet just blew off the bench.
interrupts.missNote: The sheet sat in the chip pan through the rest of the setup. The first article got measured against a tolerance recalled from memory, and it was the band for the previous revision of this print, not the current one.
interrupts.why: The whole dry run is being checked against numbers on that sheet — the offset, the tolerance, the fixture callouts. Face-down in a chip pan, it stops being something anyone can actually re-check, and the next number pulled from memory instead of the page is exactly how a setup drifts off the print without anyone deciding it should.
interrupts.wrongNote: That's not the sheet — it's down by the chip pan, not still on the bench.

lateNotes.cycle-start: Cycle start comes after the dry run, the offsets and the door — a first cut on an unproven setup is the crash.
lateNotes.micrometer: The first article is measured after the first part is cut, not before.
lateNotes.tool-setter: The tool is measured once it is in the spindle and the machine is safe to approach.

name: CNC Cell

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the part, the fixture, the tool list, the work offset and the first-article dimensions.
steps.prompt: Check the part, the fixture, the tool list, the work offset and the first-article dimensions.
steps.title: Read the setup sheet
steps.why: The setup sheet is the contract between the programmer and the machinist, written by someone who is not standing at this machine. Everything measured, torqued or offset in this job — the fixture, the tool list, the work offset, the tolerance band — is checked against a number on this sheet, not against what looks right.

steps.cue: Stop the spindle, take the machine out of auto to manual, then lock and tag.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Stop, then manual, then lock — the motion stops before the mode changes, and the lock goes on last.
steps.prompt: Stop the spindle, take the machine out of auto to manual, then lock and tag.
steps.title: Make the machine safe to approach
steps.why: A stopped spindle is not a safe spindle while the control can still run a queued program off a cycle-start signal from anywhere on the network. Manual mode takes that queued program out of play, and the lock is what stops a second person from putting it back while a hand is in the envelope.

steps.cue: Seat the fixture on a clean table, bolt and locate it, then load the part in the vise.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Seat, then bolt, then load — the fixture is fixed before the part goes in it.
steps.prompt: Seat the fixture on a clean table, bolt and locate it, then load the part in the vise.
steps.title: Set the fixture and load the part
steps.why: Everything downstream — the tool offset, the first article, every part after it — assumes the fixture has not moved since it was located and bolted down. A single chip trapped under a fixture face is a tenth of an inch of tilt that shows up as the same error on every part cut in this run, not just the first one.

steps.cue: Bring the vise to the torque on the fixture drawing and commit inside the band.

gauge.label: CLAMP TORQUE
gauge.missNote: Off the drawing's torque — a loose part is a projectile and a crushed one is scrap.

steps.prompt: Bring the vise to the torque on the fixture drawing and commit inside the band.
steps.title: Torque the workholding
steps.why: Under-clamped, the part rides up under cutting load and comes out of the vise at cutting speed, taking the tool with it. Over-clamped, thin-wall stock distorts under the jaw pressure and springs back the moment the clamp is released, so a part that measured perfectly in the vise is out of tolerance the second it's free.

steps.cue: Check the insert, the holder and the pull stud, then load the tool into the spindle.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Inspect first, then load — a cracked insert found after the tool is in the spindle was found one step too late.
steps.prompt: Check the insert, the holder and the pull stud, then load the tool into the spindle.
steps.title: Inspect and load the tool
steps.why: A cracked insert or a loose pull stud is invisible once the tool is buried in the holder and turning at spindle speed. At that speed either one becomes shrapnel inside a sheet-metal enclosure built to contain chips and coolant, not a piece of tooling that has come apart under load.

steps.cue: Get your hands and your tools out of the envelope, then remove your lock and tag.
steps.prompt: Get your hands and your tools out of the envelope, then remove your lock and tag.
steps.title: Take your lock off before anything moves
steps.why: Your lock, your call — nobody takes it off but you, and it comes off only once the envelope is empty. Everything from the tool setter onwards moves the machine, and none of it happens with a lock hanging on it.

steps.cue: Touch the tool off on the setter and commit the length offset inside the band.

gauge.label: TOOL LENGTH
gauge.missNote: Offset outside the expected range — re-touch it off before anything moves under program.

steps.prompt: Touch the tool off on the setter and commit the length offset inside the band.
steps.title: Measure the tool and set the offset
steps.why: The length offset is the one number that tells the control exactly where the tip of this specific tool sits relative to the part zero. Wrong by a tenth of an inch and the very first programmed move either cuts nothing but air or drives the tool straight through the fixture before anyone can react.

steps.cue: Run the program single-block at reduced feed with the tool held clear above the part.
steps.holdBreakNote: Feed override out of band — at that rate you cannot stop before a crash. Bring it back and hold.
steps.prompt: Run the program single-block at reduced feed with the tool held clear above the part.
steps.title: Single-block dry run above the part
steps.why: The dry run is where a wrong offset, a missed clamp or a rapid into the fixture shows up harmlessly. Every setup gets one, every time, and it is held above the part so a mistake costs nothing.

steps.cue: Close the enclosure door and confirm the interlock is made before cycle start.
steps.prompt: Close the enclosure door and confirm the interlock is made before cycle start.
steps.title: Close the door
steps.why: The enclosure is the guard, not decoration around the machine. Closed and interlocked, it contains a part or a broken tool that comes loose under cutting load; left open, it is simply a window a piece of metal leaves through at whatever speed the spindle was turning when it let go.

steps.cue: Turn the control to auto and start the cycle, staying at the panel through the first part.
steps.prompt: Turn the control to auto and start the cycle, staying at the panel through the first part.
steps.title: Run the first part
steps.why: The operator stays at the panel with a hand near feed hold for the whole first part, watching the cut and listening to it, because the first part is the one that finds whatever mistake the dry run couldn't — a clamp that was fine in the air but not under load, an offset that was close enough to pass the touch-off but not the cut.

steps.cue: Take the critical dimension with the micrometer and commit inside the drawing tolerance.

gauge.label: BORE DIA
gauge.missNote: Outside the drawing tolerance — adjust the offset and cut another before the run continues.

steps.prompt: Take the critical dimension with the micrometer and commit inside the drawing tolerance.
steps.title: Measure the first article
steps.why: The first article is what says the setup makes good parts. Nothing else in the run is measured until this one is signed off, because everything after it is a copy of it.

steps.cue: Take the brush and the chip vacuum to the nest on the table.

drag.missNote: Not on the nest — bring the brush down onto the chips on the table.

steps.prompt: Take the brush and the chip vacuum to the nest on the table.
steps.title: Clear the chips properly
steps.why: A brush and a vacuum, never air and never a bare hand — chips off a machine still carry the heat of the cut and a stringer wraps around whatever touches it. That single habit, repeated every time without exception, is most of what separates a machinist who keeps all ten fingers from one who doesn't.

steps.cue: Check the coolant, the covers and the panel, and click anything that will not survive a full run.

itemNotes.coolant-low: The coolant sight glass is below minimum — the tool will burn and the chips will not clear.
itemNotes.way-cover-torn: The Z-axis way cover is split, which lets chips into the ways and scores them under load.

steps.prompt: Check the coolant, the covers and the panel, and click anything that will not survive a full run.
steps.title: Walk the machine before the run
steps.why: A production run is hours of largely unattended cutting once it's turned loose. Coolant that's marginal now runs dry by the fiftieth part, and a way cover that's split now is packed with swarf and scoring the ways by the hundredth — walked and caught here, either one is a five-minute fix instead of a ruined slide.

tagline: Machining centre setup and first part: setup sheet, spindle stopped and locked before the envelope, workholding torqued, tool measured and offset, single-block dry run above the part, door closed, first article measured, chips brushed not blown
